summary: For ages 5–7, teach that dinosaurs came in a huge RANGE of sizes — some as tall as a house or long as a bus, others as small as a chicken — by comparing dinosaurs to familiar referents (a child, a bus, a house, a chicken) using comparative language (taller than, longer than, heavier than, smaller than). The central insight is the range itself, not absolute metres or tonnes, so always pair a giant with a tiny dinosaur. Keep comparisons at a shared scale so they are fair.
misconceptions: 'All dinosaurs were enormous' — many were small; some were chicken- or turkey-sized.
'The scariest/meat-eaters were the biggest' — the very largest were plant-eating long-necks; some carnivores were tiny.
'Dinosaurs were all bigger than any animal today' — small dinosaurs were the size of familiar small animals.
'Bigger dinosaur means it lived more recently / is more advanced' — size is not a timeline.
'Pictures show real relative size' when objects aren't drawn to a common scale — fair comparison needs the same scale.

activities.title: Compare dinosaurs to your own world (scale stage)
steps: Place a chosen familiar object on a comparison stage: yourself (a child figure), a bus, a house, and a chicken.

Bring a dinosaur alongside the chosen object at the same shared scale and look at how they compare — e.g. Brachiosaurus reaching past the roof of a house, Compsognathus barely bigger than the chicken.
Say or complete a comparison out loud: 'Brachiosaurus is taller than the house', 'Compsognathus is smaller than a big dog'.
Use a 'stand next to it' option to drop a small version of yourself beside each dinosaur and say how it compares to you ('its leg is taller than me!').
Deliberately compare a giant and a tiny dinosaur one after the other so you feel the contrast.
activities.insight: Dinosaurs ranged from chicken-sized to house-sized; not all were huge. Size is a relation you understand by comparing to familiar things at the same scale.

activities.title: Order dinosaurs from smallest to biggest
steps: Take a jumbled set of several dinosaurs (including a chicken-sized one and a long-necked giant) and arrange them in a line from shortest to longest (smallest to largest by length).
Say which is smallest and which is largest, and name one of each if you can (e.g. Compsognathus small, Brachiosaurus large).
Attach or say a comparative word for each neighbouring pair (this one is longer than that one).
activities.insight: Dinosaurs can be ordered by size, and the full spread runs from tiny to gigantic.

activities.title: To-scale line-up poster (scaffold)
steps: Look at a poster where dinosaurs are drawn beside a bus, a house, and a child at the same shared scale.
Point to each dinosaur and read or say its comparison: 'as tall as a house', 'as small as a chicken'.
Find the biggest and the smallest on the poster and describe the difference.
activities.insight: A fair comparison uses a common scale, and a single picture can show the full range at once.

activities.title: Check the 'all dinosaurs were giant' idea
steps: Respond to a friend who says: 'ALL dinosaurs were gigantic — as big as a house or bigger. A dinosaur the size of a chicken couldn't be a real dinosaur.' Agree or disagree, and explain.
Name one really big dinosaur and one really small dinosaur.
Answer: Was every dinosaur bigger than an elephant? What about a blue whale living today?
Finish: 'Brachiosaurus was ___ than a bus; Compsognathus was ___ than a big dog.'
activities.insight: Dinosaurs came in a huge range of sizes; a small, chicken-sized dinosaur is still a real dinosaur, and some living animals (like a blue whale) are bigger than most dinosaurs.

checkQuestion: Your friend says 'ALL dinosaurs were gigantic — as big as a house or bigger. A dinosaur the size of a chicken couldn't be a real dinosaur.' Do you agree? Explain what the range of dinosaur sizes was really like.
checkAnswer: Disagree. Dinosaurs came in a huge RANGE of sizes: some were enormous (Brachiosaurus, taller than a house), but others were tiny — as small as a chicken (like Compsognathus). A small dinosaur is still a real dinosaur, so 'all dinosaurs were gigantic' is wrong.
